newsitem.title: USA: Time Warner posts profit for quarter, loss for year.
newsitem.headline: Time Warner posts profit for quarter, loss for year.

text.p: Time Warner Inc. said Tuesday profits rose 79 percent in the fourth quarter, aided by the Turner Broadcasting System Inc. acquisition and three hit movies, although its losses grew for the full year.

The New York-based communications giant said net income jumped to $59 million in the quarter ended Dec. 31, although that translated to a loss of 3 cents a share after payment of preferred dividends, compared with a profit of $33 million, or 1 cent a share, in the 1995 quarter.

Results were boosted by strong showings at Home Box Office and the cable television business at Turner, as well as the movies "Twister," "Eraser" and "A Time To Kill", which each pulled in more than $100 million at the box office.
Time Warner said that was a first in movie history.
The company also said that Warner Bros. television continued to lead the ratings with the hit shows "ER" and "Friends," and one of the season's new hits, "Suddenly Susan."

Analysts said they were encouraged by earnings growth in the company's publishing, cable television and film divisions. Weakness in the music division mirrored the lackluster state of that industry, they said.
"The numbers were great," Merrill Lynch analyst Jessica Reif said, adding that in a meeting with analysts the company offered up "a lot of focus on the bottom line."

Restating results to account for the merger with Turner Broadcasting, completed in October, and other acquisitions, cash flow rose about 12 percent, which was more than some analysts had anticipated, Reif said.
Cash flow, which measures earnings excluding interest payments, depreciation and other items, is an important measure of performance for companies with heavy debt such as Time Warner.

Analysts also said they were encouraged by the nominations of Hilton Hotels Corp. Chief Executive Stephen Bollenbach and UAL Corp. Chairman Gerald Greenwald to Time Warner's board of directors. Bollenbach and Greenwald are viewed as aggressive businessmen with experience in restructurings.
Bollenbach, a former chief financial officer at Walt Disney Co., could help Time Warner digest Turner Broadcasting. He is currently heading Hilton's $6.5 billion bid for ITT Corp.
Time Warner Chief Executive Gerald Levin said the integration with Turner Broadcasting was "strategically complete" and that he expected a record-setting year in 1997.
For the full year, Time Warner said it lost $191 million, or $1.04 a share, up from a loss of $166 million, or 57 cents a share, in 1995.
The results included losses of $35 million in 1996 and $42 million in 1995 from retirement of debt.
Revenues grew 31 percent to $6.7 billion from $5.1 billion in the quarter and 18 percent to $20.9 billion from $17.7 billion for the year.
Time Warner said its fourth-quarter earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, or cash flow, rose 34 percent to a record $1.4 billion from $1.0 billion.
For the full year, cash flow expanded 30 percent to a record $4.3 billion from $3.3 billion.
The company said cash flow improved at all its major businesses in the quarter, with HBO up 25 percent, Time Inc. up 14 percent and Time Warner Cable up 32 percent.

Time Warner said the performance of the Turner Networks remained outstanding. TNT, CNN and the TBS Superstation now reach over 70 million households each and the Cartoon Network is in 40 million homes, the company said.
Time Warner's stock rose $1.875 to $41.50 on the New York Stock Exchange.
